items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Some researchers have adopted a 20 kg upper limit to avian predation on primates, with no confirmed cases exceeding 13 kg. Here, we report evidence of eagle interactions with adult male olive baboons (
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                        <jats:italic>Papio anubis</jats:italic>
                      </jats:styled-content>
                      ) and evaluate the implications for understanding past predation pressures during hominin evolution.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fieldwork was conducted in Réserve Naturelle et Culturelle d'Ennedi, Chad, in February–March 2025. Surveys of sandstone cliffs and talus deposits yielded cranial and postcranial remains of
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                        <jats:italic>P. anubis</jats:italic>
                      </jats:styled-content>
                      , including proximal femora. We measured the superoinferior breadth of each femoral head to estimate body mass using established cercopithecid regression equations. The remains were examined for taphonomic signatures of eagle predation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our sample of nine individuals includes eight adult males with a mean estimated body mass of 22.2 ± 3.8 kg. We observed punctured orbits in two males, along with a raked scapula, two telling signs of eagle predation and/or feeding activity. One male was associated with a femur, enabling a body mass estimate of 21.8 kg. Postscript: in June 2026, we recovered the cranium and partial skeleton of an adult male with an estimated body mass of 26.2 kg; and again, we observed evidence of talon punctures and severe raking of the scapulae.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Our findings are consistent with the depredations of Verreaux's eagles (
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                        <jats:italic>Aquila verreauxii</jats:italic>
                      </jats:styled-content>
                      ). If confirmed, the interaction exceeds the primate body‐mass threshold deemed susceptible to avian predation, indicating that moderately large primates, including some hominins, may have experienced greater avian predation pressure than previously recognized.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Catherine Hobaiter, Tewogbade J. D. Akpona, Gisela H. Kopp, Nathaniel J. Dominy

items.abstract: Build orientation for selective laser melting (SLM) manufacturing of dental parts is usually chosen manually by technicians. We treat orientation prediction as supervised machine learning of the part's up-axis from technician-labeled production data, and test which rotation representations produce the best results. Using $n\approx2400$ patient-specific dental parts, we trained a ResNet-50 multi-view image backbone and a PointNeXt-S point-cloud backbone, both pretrained and fine-tuned end-to-end, on 13 up-axis representations spanning six classical $SO(3)$ parameterizations and seven representations defined directly on the unit sphere $S^2$. We report the geodesic angular error between predicted and ground-truth up-axis on a test set, with and without test-time augmentation (TTA) over $K=21$ known rotations. With TTA, the octahedral map achieves the lowest mean angular error ($10.6^\circ$, ResNet-50). The three lowest-error results overall are direct $S^2$ representations, though this may reflect label noise in the unsupervised in-plane component of the $SO(3)$ targets rather than a topological advantage. von Mises-Fisher collapses to a near-constant prediction when trained with PointNeXt-S but not with ResNet-50. TTA reduces mean angular error by 31-73 % across almost every representation and backbone. Overall, test-time augmentation over a small set of known rotations is the most consistent driver of accuracy, whereas the best-performing representation is strongly backbone-dependent.

items.title: Predicting build orientation for SLM dental parts: a comparison of rotation representations and direct vector regression

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The study of dogs (
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:italic>Canis familiaris</jats:italic>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    ) in the Byzantine Empire is under‐developed relative to earlier and more western portions of the Roman world, largely due to their archeological rarity. Salvage excavations beginning in 2004 in the Yenikapı neighborhood of Istanbul over the former Harbor of Theodosius however retrieved the remains of several hundred dogs from the Byzantine period of the City, providing exceptional opportunity for dedicated study. Here, we present the first 3D geometric morphometric assessment of this large assemblage, which aimed to investigate the prevailing phenotypic character of the dogs of Constantinople during the Early and Middle Byzantine periods (7th–12th centuries
                    <jats:sc>AD</jats:sc>
                    ). Similar to prior assessments, we determined that most of these dogs were small, mesocephalic individuals of a generic and unspecialised appearance. Of modern dogs, they are nearest to members of the Spitz–Primitive group, most of which are unspecialised varieties with origins as free‐ranging village and pariah‐types. A smaller proportion of the Byzantine dogs however show close similarities to specialized dog breed groups historically associated with specific working purposes, such as livestock guardian dogs, sighthounds, and terriers. We conclude that the dog population of Constantinople as represented by those which ended up in the Theodosian Harbor was diverse in its overall range of observed phenotypes but was dominated by a prevailing unspecialised morphotype that is reminiscent of the free‐ranging street dogs historically known from the city.
                  </jats:p>
items.summary: 《伊斯坦布尔耶尼卡珀狄奥多西港拜占庭时期犬类颅骨表型的3D几何形态测量分析》：该研究首次对伊斯坦布尔耶尼卡珀狄奥多西港遗址出土的数百只拜占庭时期犬类遗存进行3D几何形态测量，旨在探究7至12世纪君士坦丁堡犬群的主要表型特征，发现其以小型、中头型且外观非特化的个体为主，与现代斯皮茨—原始犬组最为接近，另有少数与牲畜护卫犬、视觉猎犬和梗犬等专业犬种相似，值得关…

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Barro Alto fossil site (Rio Grande do Sul State, Brazil) is considered a prolific place for understanding the Guadalupian (Wordian) vertebrate diversity, especially for tetrapods and cartilaginous fishes. However, its paleoenvironmental context has not been deeply discussed in the literature. The present work aims to integrate previous and new paleontological data for this fossiliferous site and provide the depositional context for the Permian fauna of the Rio do Rasto Formation (Paraná Basin) at the Barro Alto site. The stratigraphic columnar profile is divided into six sedimentary facies grouped into two facies associations, which were integrated with paleontological and petrological data. The association of facies suggests that the paleoenvironmental context for the Barro Alto fossil site consists of a lacustrine paleoenvironment with seasonal variations in water levels and sediment influx, being eventually invaded by river channels. Furthermore, it contained a remarkable diversity of vertebrate remains, with bony (both Actinopterygii and Sarcopterygii) and cartilaginous fishes, terrestrial tetrapods from different groups such as anomodont synapsids, archosauromorphs, and temnospondyls, besides coprolites and plant remains. Additionally, recent paleontological studies involving the Karoo basin in South Africa may suggest a geochronological repositioning of the Barro Alto site to the Wordian due to biostratigraphic relationships between South African and Brazilian taxa.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Relationships between chronological age and skeletal and dental indicators of growth and development have largely contributed to shaping our approaches to subadult age estimation in biological anthropology. Dental development has historically been considered the most accurate age indicator. This somewhat suppositional appreciation of the predictive capability of age indicators conflates genetic potential (a biological phenomenon) with predictive power (a statistical phenomenon). Further, indicators of growth and development are scored or assessed differently (i.e., continuous vs. ordinal data). This data complexity further convolutes the relationship between indicator and estimates. The current study uses information theory to better understand the relationships of skeletal and dental growth and development indicators with age across postnatal ontogeny and evaluate their respective predictive power.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sixty‐two indicators including long bone measurements, epiphyseal fusion stages, and dental development stages were recorded for 1317 contemporary male and female US individuals aged between birth and 21 years. Information gain of each indicator on age was assessed using 62 univariate mixed cumulative probit (MCP) models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Each variable provides varying levels of information to age throughout the subadult period. Patterns of information gain mirror developmental trajectories (i.e., growth velocity, fusion/mineralization activity), are sexually dimorphic, and are affected by the data type and precision in data collection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings challenge the idea of a best indicator or variable for subadult age estimation, elucidate the complex patterns of age‐related relationships during ontogeny, and corroborate multivariate and multi‐indicator age estimation models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Kyra E. Stull, Louise K. Corron, Elaine Y. Chu, Michael H. Price, Christopher A. Wolfe

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The skull of carnivorans represents a highly integrated anatomical structure shaped by selective pressures associated with feeding ecology, sensory specialization, locomotion, and phylogenetic history. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of craniomandibular morphometric indices in the order
                    <jats:italic>Carnivora</jats:italic>
                    , integrating their anatomical definitions, morphometric foundations, and functional significance. Standardized cranial and mandibular measurements are reviewed together with 11 widely used proportional indices, including the Cranial Index (CI), Skull Index (SI), Facial Index (FI), Facial Length Index (FLI), Cranial Length Index (CLI), Cranial Height Index (CHI), Orbital Index (OI), Palatal Index (PI), Foramen Magnum Index (FMI), Mandibular Body Index (MBI), and Mandibular Ramus Index (MRI). The review highlights the biomechanical and evolutionary relevance of these indices by examining their relationships with bite performance, craniofacial organization, sensory adaptations, feeding ecology, and morphological diversification among carnivoran families. In addition to summarizing published morphometric indices, several proportional indices that have rarely been reported as independent variables are derived from previously published linear craniometric measurements, providing standardized quantitative descriptors for comparative analyses across species. By compiling anatomical landmarks, measurement protocols, functional interpretations, and comparative data within a unified framework, this review identifies current knowledge gaps and promotes greater methodological consistency in future studies. Although some proportional indices were calculated from published measurements rather than directly reported in the original literature, they provide valuable complementary metrics for evaluating cranial and mandibular morphology. Overall, the integration of these 11 morphometric indices offers a comprehensive approach for investigating craniofacial evolution, functional morphology, feeding adaptations, and taxonomic diversity in both extant and fossil carnivorans. This review provides a practical reference for researchers in comparative anatomy, evolutionary biology, paleontology, and veterinary morphology.
                  </jats:p>

items.title: A comprehensive review of craniomandibular morphometric indices in carnivora: Anatomical basis, functional significance, and comparative applications
